name: Electric Water Heater
blurb: A standard electric tank water heater is typically the second-largest energy user in an all-electric home, burning 10–15 kWh a day for a family's showers, laundry, and dishes. Its 4,500-watt elements run about three hours a day in aggregate.
tips: Set the thermostat to 120°F — hotter settings cost more and raise scald risk.
Low-flow showerheads pay for themselves in weeks on electric hot water.
If your utility offers a water-heater timer or off-peak program, a tank stores heat beautifully — enroll.

name: Tankless Electric Water Heater
blurb: Whole-house electric tankless units draw a startling 13–27 kW while a tap runs — often the largest instantaneous load in the house — but only run during actual hot-water use. Total monthly energy usually lands modestly below an equivalent tank by eliminating standby losses.

name: Heat Pump Water Heater
blurb: Heat pump water heaters pull heat from surrounding air, delivering hot water on roughly one-third the electricity of a standard electric tank. For most all-electric homes, this is the single biggest bill reduction one appliance swap can make.

name: Hot Tub
blurb: Between the heater and circulation pumps, a typical outdoor hot tub consumes 3–8 kWh per day — more in winter, less with a quality cover. It's routinely a top-five household load that owners forget to count.
tips: A tight-fitting insulated cover is the single biggest cost lever — most heat loss is from the water surface.
Drop the setpoint a few degrees between soaks rather than powering fully down and reheating.
In winter, wind exposure matters; a fence or enclosure measurably cuts heater runtime.

name: Pool Pump
blurb: A single-speed pool pump running eight hours a day is one of the most expensive devices at any home that has one — often rivaling central AC across a season. Variable-speed pumps do the same filtration for 50–80% less energy and pay for themselves quickly.
tips: Replace single-speed pumps with variable-speed — it's the highest-ROI pool upgrade available.
Most residential pools filter adequately in 6 hours, not 12; test shorter runtimes.
Run the pump off-peak if your utility has time-of-use pricing.

name: Pool Heater (Heat Pump)
blurb: Heat pump pool heaters draw 4–11 kW while running, and extending a swim season can add more to a bill than every indoor appliance combined. A solar cover that holds overnight heat is the difference between occasional top-ups and daily multi-hour runs.

name: Well Pump
blurb: A typical ¾–1 HP well pump draws about 1,000–1,500 watts and runs whenever the pressure tank calls for water. A pump that short-cycles or runs constantly usually signals a leak or waterlogged tank — and shows up as a mystery bill increase.

name: Sump Pump
blurb: Sump pumps draw substantial power but run only when water arrives — minutes a day in dry spells, hours during storms. A pump running constantly in dry weather points to a stuck float or drainage problem, not a normal bill.

name: Aquarium
blurb: Between the heater, filter, and lighting, a mid-size heated aquarium averages 50–150 watts continuously — comparable to a refrigerator over a month. Big reef tanks with pumps and intense lighting can triple that.

name: Hot/Cold Water Dispenser
blurb: Bottle-style dispensers keep a hot tank and a cold tank ready around the clock, averaging about 100 watts. Switching off the hot side (or using a timer) can cut its consumption roughly in half.
